# Title: Kururin Squash\! A Comprehensive Analysis of Gameplay, Development, and Market Performance
## 1\. Executive Summary
*Kururin Squash\!* (Japanese: くるりんスカッシュ！, Hepburn: *Kururin Sukasshu\!*) stands as a pivotal yet often overlooked artifact in the library of the Nintendo GameCube. Developed by Eighting and published by Nintendo, the title was released exclusively in Japan on October 14, 2004\. It represents the third and final installment in the *Kururin* trilogy, succeeding the Game Boy Advance titles *Kuru Kuru Kururin* (2001) and *Kururin Paradise* (2002).

This report provides an exhaustive examination of *Kururin Squash\!*, analyzing its transition from handheld 2D mechanics to console-based 3D environments, its complex ludic systems involving vehicle transformations and boss encounters, and its distinct "paper puppet" aesthetic. Furthermore, the report investigates the commercial paradox of the title: despite receiving critical acclaim for its polished mechanics and accessibility—garnering high praise from import-focused Western outlets and respectable scores from Japanese publications like *Famitsu*—it became the lowest-selling entry in the franchise. The analysis explores the factors contributing to this market performance, including its late-generation release timing, the specific demographics of the GameCube user base, and the lack of international localization.

Through a synthesis of production credits, sales data, and critical reception, this document establishes *Kururin Squash\!* not merely as a puzzle game, but as a significant case study in Nintendo's experimental phase during the early 2000s—a period characterized by high-quality, niche titles that prioritized creative gameplay loops over mass-market trends.

## 2\. Historical Context and Development
### 2.1 The *Kururin* Lineage
To fully appreciate the design philosophy of *Kururin Squash\!*, one must situate it within the broader context of the *Kururin* series. The franchise began in 2001 with *Kuru Kuru Kururin*, a launch title for the Game Boy Advance. The core concept was deceptively simple: guide a slowly rotating stick (the Helirin) through a maze without touching the walls. This mechanic required a unique blend of rhythm, spatial awareness, and patience. The sequel, *Kururin Paradise* (2002), expanded on this foundation with faster gameplay and more intricate level designs.

*Kururin Squash\!* arrived two years later, marking the series' first and only foray onto a home console. This transition was significant. The Game Boy Advance hardware relied on sprite-based graphics and lacked the processing power for complex physics simulations or 3D rendering. The move to the Nintendo GameCube offered the developers at Eighting the computational resources to reinvent the series' presentation and mechanics. The result was a game that retained the 2D planar movement of its predecessors but enveloped it in a fully realized 3D world, complete with dynamic lighting, particle effects, and physics-based interactions .

### 2.2 Production and Staffing
The development of *Kururin Squash\!* was spearheaded by a veteran team at Eighting, working in close collaboration with Nintendo. The project was led by directors **Shinji Hatano** and **Tomonori Fujisawa**, who orchestrated the transition of the franchise to 3D . The production was overseen by producers **Hiroshi Sato** and **Masato Toyoshima**, ensuring that the title met Nintendo's stringent quality standards .

A critical component of the game's identity was its audio-visual presentation. The musical score was composed by **Atsuhiro Motoyama**, whose work on the previous *Kururin* titles had established the series' upbeat, electronic soundscape . For *Squash\!*, Motoyama utilized the GameCube's superior audio hardware to create a richer, more instrumentally diverse soundtrack that complemented the vibrant visuals.

The artistic vision was executed by a team of designers including **Nanako Kinoshita**, **Tomomi Sano**, **Ryuusuke Yoshida**, and **Takayoshi Matsui**.4 They were tasked with translating the 2D character designs of **Yoichi Kotabe**—a legendary artist known for his work on the *Super Mario* and *Pokémon* franchises—into a format that worked within a 3D game engine. Their solution was a distinctive "paper puppet" style, where characters appeared as 2D cutouts moving within 3D environments, a stylistic choice that preserved the series' 2D roots while leveraging the console's polygon-pushing capabilities .

The inclusion of **Masahiro Yuge** in the planning department is noteworthy. Yuge, having worked on the course design for previous entries, provided a continuity of design logic, ensuring that despite the new gimmicks and 3D graphics, the "soul" of the level design remained faithful to the series' challenging origins .

## 3\. Gameplay Mechanics and Systems
### 3.1 Core Physics and Control Scheme
At its heart, *Kururin Squash\!* is an action-puzzle game that demands precision. The player controls the **Helirin**, a helicopter-like vehicle that resembles a long, spinning stick. Unlike traditional vehicles in gaming that move linearly, the Helirin rotates clockwise at a constant speed. The player must navigate this rotating object through narrow corridors, complex mazes, and hazard-filled chambers.

The challenge arises from the geometry of the levels relative to the Helirin. The corridors are often narrower than the diameter of the Helirin's rotation. To pass through, the player must time their movement so that the Helirin is aligned parallel to the corridor walls at the exact moment of passage. This rhythmic interplay between movement and rotation creates a unique "flow" state, where the player acts not just as a pilot, but as a conductor of momentum .

The control scheme on the GameCube controller was designed to offer players granular control over this rotation, introducing layers of complexity absent in a simple passive-rotation system:

* **Analog Movement**: The GameCube's analog stick allows for fluid, omnidirectional movement, a significant upgrade from the 8-way directional pad of the GBA, offering smoother acceleration and deceleration curves. 
* **Rotation Acceleration (R Button)**: By holding the **R button**, the player can double the speed of the Helirin's rotation. This is not merely for patience management; it is a critical gameplay mechanic. Faster rotation allows the Helirin to "fit" through rapidly changing gaps and increases the frequency of attacks when using offensive power-ups . 
* **Speed Boost (B Button)**: Holding the **B button** increases the Helirin's travel speed. This risk-reward mechanic allows skilled players to bypass obstacles quickly but reduces the window of reaction time for upcoming hazards . 
* **Rotation Reversal (Springs)**: The environment itself acts as a controller input. Blue springs scattered throughout the levels instantly reverse the direction of the Helirin's rotation (e.g., from clockwise to counter-clockwise). Mastering these reversal points is essential for navigating S-bends and other complex geometries where a constant rotation direction would result in a collision .

### 3.2 Health and Penalty Systems
*Kururin Squash\!* employs a health-based failure state, distinct from the strict time-penalty systems seen in some puzzle genres. The Helirin is equipped with a set of "hearts"—typically three at the start of a level.

* **Collision Consequence**: Upon colliding with a wall or an enemy, the Helirin takes damage, losing one heart. The player experiences a brief invulnerability period or recoil, disrupting their rhythm . 
* **Critical Failure**: If all hearts are depleted, the Helirin "shatters," and the level ends. The player must restart from the beginning or from a checkpoint if they have utilized an "Amazing Heart" item . 
* **Recovery and Upgrades**: Players can extend their survivability by purchasing "Heart-Ups" (increasing the maximum heart count to five) or finding recovery items within the levels .

This system creates a tension between speed and safety. While the primary goal is often simply to reach the exit, the presence of a timer and the "Perfect" rating system (requiring no damage and full coin collection) encourages players to optimize their routes, often at the risk of taking damage .

### 3.3 Vehicle Transformations (The "Squash" Mechanics)
The defining innovation of *Kururin Squash\!* is the introduction of specialized Helirin variants. These distinct vehicles are not merely cosmetic; they fundamentally alter the player's interaction with the game world, transforming the genre from pure avoidance to active engagement and combat. These transformations are thematic to the specific worlds in which they appear.

#### 3.3.1 Helibokaan (Boxing Helirin)
Introduced in the "Sweet Shores" world, the **Helibokaan** (sometimes referred to as "Helibash" in translations) equips the Helirin with extendable boxing gloves on its tips.

* **Mechanic**: Pressing the **A button** extends the gloves. 
* **Utility**: This allows the player to smash through cracked walls, destroy obstacles, and engage in combat with enemies. 
* **Economic Incentive**: Successfully punching enemies or objects often releases coins, integrating combat directly into the game's economy . 
* **Strategic Depth**: The punch extends the Helirin's reach effectively, meaning players must calculate a larger collision radius when attacking, but a smaller one when navigating tight spaces .

#### 3.3.2 Helibashan (Submarine Helirin)
Used in water-themed stages, the **Helibashan** introduces verticality to the 2D plane.

* **Mechanic**: Pressing the **A button** causes the Helirin to dive underwater. 
* **Utility**: While submerged, the Helirin can pass underneath surface-level obstacles such as floating logs, low bridges, or enemies. 
* **Critique**: Some critics noted that this mechanic felt the most passive of the new additions, as it focused on evasion rather than the satisfying feedback of combat found in other transformations .

#### 3.3.3 Heliboboh (Flamethrower Helirin)
The **Heliboboh** transforms the Helirin into a mobile weapon platform equipped with flamethrowers.

* **Mechanic**: The player must aim and fire streams of flame. 
* **Utility**: This is essential for melting ice barriers in frozen levels and defeating specific enemies that are vulnerable only to fire. 
* **Challenge**: The rotation of the Helirin makes aiming difficult. Players must time their bursts of fire to align with the rotation, creating a "strafe and shoot" dynamic unique to this title .

#### 3.3.4 Heliburuun (Tornado Helirin)
Perhaps the most chaotic transformation, the **Heliburuun** allows the player to generate and launch miniature tornadoes.

* **Mechanic**: The player charges the mechanism and releases a projectile tornado. 
* **Utility**: Tornadoes can travel across the screen to activate distant switches, clear hazards, or interact with enemies that are physically unreachable due to walls or pits. This adds a puzzle-solving layer where the player must calculate the trajectory of the projectile relative to the Helirin's spin .

#### 3.3.5 Helibibyuun (Racing Helirin)
The **Helibibyuun** is designed for speed.

* **Utility**: Used in high-speed racing segments, this vehicle has enhanced acceleration and top speed characteristics, shifting the gameplay focus from puzzle-solving to reflex-based twitch gameplay .

### 3.4 Boss Battles
A significant departure from the GBA games is the inclusion of boss battles at the conclusion of each world. These encounters are not simple mazes but structured fights against large, mechanical adversaries piloted or controlled by the antagonist, Professor Isogashima .

* **Combat Integration**: The bosses require the player to use the specific Helirin of that world. For example, the first boss requires the use of the **Helibokaan** to punch through the boss's defenses and strike its weak point . 
* **Pattern Recognition**: Like traditional action games, players must memorize attack patterns and wait for openings, all while maintaining the constant rotation of the Helirin to avoid taking damage .

## 4\. Narrative and World Building
### 4.1 Premise and Characters
The narrative of *Kururin Squash\!* is lighthearted, whimsical, and steeped in "typical Japanese wackiness" . It utilizes a cast of anthropomorphic animal characters to tell a story of family and rescue.

* **Kururin**: The protagonist, a blue bird who pilots the Helirin. He is characterized by his determination to save his family . 
* **The Family**: The story begins with Kururin's family—including his mother (**Kakarin**), father (**Totorin**), and ten siblings—winning a lottery for a cruise vacation across four countries . 
* **Professor Hare**: A recurring ally (also known as Teacher Hare), a genius inventor who creates the specialized Helirins to aid Kururin's journey . 
* **Professor Isogashima**: The primary antagonist (also referred to as Dr. Gash). A mad scientist with a chaotic desire to "make everyone busy" and stop Kururin from interfering with his research. He is responsible for kidnapping Kururin's family .

### 4.2 Plot Progression
Upon returning from the prize vacation, Kururin discovers that his siblings are missing. Professor Isogashima has scattered them across the four countries they visited. Kururin must retrace the path of the cruise, navigating through the distinct environments of each country to rescue his siblings .

After successfully rescuing all siblings, a plot twist occurs: Kururin returns home to find that his parents, Kakarin and Totorin, have also been abducted. Isogashima has taken them to the **Wonderverse**, a fifth world set in outer space . Kururin travels to this final frontier for a climatic showdown. Upon Isogashima's defeat, the villain crash-lands and, in a comedic resolution, decides to reform by "making himself busy" fixing the trouble he caused. The family is reunited, unlocking the "Dad" time attack records for replayability .

### 4.3 Environmental Themes
The game is divided into distinct worlds, each featuring unique aesthetics and hazards:

1. **Sweet Shores**: A candy and tropical-themed world where the boxing mechanic is introduced. 
2. **Water World**: Featuring submarine gameplay mechanics. 
3. **Ice/Machine World**: Where the flamethrower mechanics are pivotal. 
4. **Wonderverse**: The final space-themed abstract world containing the most difficult puzzles and the final boss .

## 5\. Visual and Auditory Presentation
### 5.1 The "Paper Puppet" Aesthetic
*Kururin Squash\!* adopts a unique visual style that distinguishes it from the cel-shaded or photorealistic trends of the era. The characters are rendered as 2D flat artwork, but they exist within a fully 3D world.

* **Animation Technique**: The characters move like paper puppets on sticks. When a character turns or changes expression, the flat model flips over to reveal a different drawing on the reverse side. This "cardboard cutout" aesthetic gives the cutscenes a charming, storybook quality . 
* **3D Environments**: While the gameplay plane is 2D, the environments are fully polygonal 3D. This depth is used for visual flair, such as seeing butterflies fluttering in a forest far below the glass floor of the maze, or enemies being launched into the foreground when defeated by a tornado . 
* **Lighting and Effects**: The GameCube's hardware allowed for advanced lighting effects. Lasers cast halos of light, explosions generate particle clouds, and water surfaces have realistic transparency. These effects serve not just as eye candy but as visual feedback for the player's actions .

### 5.2 Sound Design
The audio landscape, crafted by **Atsuhiro Motoyama**, is integral to the "flow" of the game. The soundtrack features upbeat, rhythmic electronic music that matches the constant rotation of the Helirin. Sound effects are punchy and distinct—the *thwack* of the boxing glove, the *whoosh* of the flamethrower, and the shattering glass sound of a destroyed Helirin provide immediate auditory feedback .

## 6\. Commercial Performance and Market Analysis
### 6.1 Sales Figures
Despite its quality, *Kururin Squash\!* was a commercial disappointment.

* **Launch Performance**: In its debut week (October 14, 2004), the game charted at \#18 in Japan, selling only **5,745 copies**.4 
* **Lifetime Sales**: The game quickly fell out of the charts, accumulating a total of approximately **18,562 copies** sold by the end of 2004 . 
* **Comparative Ranking**: This performance made it the lowest-selling entry in the *Kururin* series. Furthermore, it holds the dubious distinction of being the second lowest-selling first-party Nintendo title on the GameCube in Japan, outperforming only *Eternal Darkness: Sanity's Requiem*.4

### 6.2 Factors Contributing to Low Sales
Several factors likely contributed to this poor market performance:

1. **Platform Lifecycle**: By late 2004, the GameCube was struggling against the dominance of the PlayStation 2\. The audience that remained was often focused on major franchises (Zelda, Mario, Metroid) rather than experimental puzzle games. 
2. **Niche Genre**: The "irritating stick" genre (a reference to the Japanese game show segment *Iraira Bou*) is inherently niche. While popular on handhelds for short bursts of play, it was a harder sell as a home console experience requiring dedicated TV time. 
3. **Lack of International Release**: The game was never released in North America or Europe. While the GBA title *Kuru Kuru Kururin* had a European release, the GameCube sequel remained Japan-exclusive. This limited its potential audience strictly to the Japanese market and a small community of importers .

## 7\. Critical Reception
### 7.1 Domestic Reviews (Japan)
In Japan, the game received respectable scores, though it was not hailed as a masterpiece.

* **Famitsu**: The prestigious magazine *Famitsu* awarded the game a score of roughly **30/40** (averaging 7.5/10), with individual reviewers giving it scores of 8s and 7s . Reviewers praised the polished mechanics and the transition to 3D but likely found the content volume or difficulty curve to be barriers to a higher score.

### 7.2 Western Import Reviews
Interestingly, Western critics who imported the game often rated it higher than their Japanese counterparts, charmed by its unique mechanics and lack of language barrier.

* **Nintendo World Report**: Awarded the game a stellar **9.5/10**. The reviewer called it "excellent" and praised the "incredible graphic style" and "lastability," recommending it unreservedly to puzzle fans . 
* **IGN**: Provided a glowing playtest, describing the experience as "addictive" and stating, "We can't stop playing this thing." They highlighted the multiplayer mode as a potential "riot" and urged Nintendo of America to localize it . 
* **Other Outlets**: *Eurogamer* gave it a **7/10**, and *Edge* gave it a **6/10**, reflecting a more critical view of its niche appeal and difficulty spikes .

### 7.3 The Language Barrier Myth
A recurring theme in Western coverage is the accessibility of the title. Despite being fully in Japanese, critics universally noted that the language barrier was "zilch" . The menus were intuitive, and the gameplay communicated its goals through visual design alone. This made *Kururin Squash\!* a staple recommendation for GameCube owners looking to import Japanese exclusives .

## 8\. Multiplayer and Replayability
### 8.1 Multiplayer Modes
*Kururin Squash\!* leverages the GameCube's four-controller ports to offer robust local multiplayer.

* **Race Mode**: Up to four players compete in split-screen to finish a stage first. This mode emphasizes speed and risk management. 
* **Battle Mode**: Players share a screen or arena, using offensive Helirins (like the boxing or tornado types) to knock opponents into walls or hazards. This chaotic mode was compared favorably to *Super Monkey Ball*'s party games .

### 8.2 The Shop and Economy
To enhance replayability, the game features a shop system run by the characters.

* **Currency**: Coins collected in levels are used here. 
* **Inventory**: Players can buy practical items like "Heart-Ups" (extra health) and "Amazing Hearts" (checkpoints), as well as cosmetic items like new Helirin colors. 
* **Minigames**: The shop also sells unlockable minigames that can be downloaded to a Game Boy Advance via the GameCube-GBA Link Cable, a feature that rewarded cross-platform ownership .

## 9\. Legacy and Cultural Impact
### 9.1 The End of a Series
*Kururin Squash\!* effectively marked the end of the *Kururin* franchise. No mainline sequel has been produced since 2004\. The commercial failure of the title likely signaled to Nintendo that the concept had reached its market ceiling. While the GBA titles were re-released on the Wii U Virtual Console, *Kururin Squash\!* remains trapped on the GameCube, never having seen a digital re-release .

### 9.2 Representation in Smash Bros.
Despite its dormancy, the series is acknowledged in Nintendo's crossover fighter, *Super Smash Bros.* The Helirin appears as a trophy/spirit, and the "Kururin" universe is cataloged in the game's archives, with *Squash\!* noted as the most recent entry .

### 9.3 Collector's Market
Today, *Kururin Squash\!* is a collector's item. Due to its low print run and Japan exclusivity, it commands a premium price. Complete copies (CIB) sell for approximately **$47**, while graded copies can reach upwards of **$146**.20 It is sought after not just for its rarity, but for its status as a high-quality, "hidden gem" of the GameCube library that showcases Nintendo's willingness to experiment with weird, wonderful concepts.

## 10\. Conclusion
*Kururin Squash\!* is a game of contradictions. It is a visually vibrant, 3D console game that plays strictly in 2D. It is a critically acclaimed title that failed commercially. It is a "casual" puzzle game with a punishing difficulty curve. Yet, these contradictions are precisely what make it a fascinating subject of study. It represents the pinnacle of the *Kururin* formula—refined, expanded, and polished to a shine—before the series was quietly retired. For those who played it, whether in Japan in 2004 or as importers years later, it remains a "delightful" and "addictive" testament to the creative spirit of the GameCube era .

The story begins with Kururin's family—including his mother (Kakarin), father (Totorin), and ten siblings—winning a lottery for a cruise vacation across four countries.
Professor Hare is a recurring ally (also known as Teacher Hare), a genius inventor who creates the specialized Helirins to aid Kururin's journey.
Professor Isogashima is the primary antagonist (also referred to as Dr. Gash) in Kururin Squash!.
Professor Isogashima is a mad scientist with a chaotic desire to "make everyone busy" and stop Kururin from interfering with his research.
Professor Isogashima is responsible for kidnapping Kururin's family.
Upon returning from the prize vacation, Kururin discovers that his siblings are missing.
Professor Isogashima has scattered Kururin's siblings across the four countries they visited.
Kururin must retrace the path of the cruise, navigating through the distinct environments of each country to rescue his siblings.
After successfully rescuing all siblings, a plot twist occurs: Kururin returns home to find that his parents, Kakarin and Totorin, have also been abducted.
Isogashima has taken Kururin's parents to the Wonderverse, a fifth world set in outer space.
Kururin travels to this final frontier for a climatic showdown.
Upon Isogashima's defeat, the villain crash-lands and, in a comedic resolution, decides to reform by "making himself busy" fixing the trouble he caused.
The family is reunited, unlocking the "Dad" time attack records for replayability.
The game is divided into distinct worlds, each featuring unique aesthetics and hazards.
Sweet Shores is a candy and tropical-themed world where the boxing mechanic is introduced.
Water World features submarine gameplay mechanics.
Ice/Machine World is where the flamethrower mechanics are pivotal.
Wonderverse is the final space-themed abstract world containing the most difficult puzzles and the final boss.
Kururin Squash! adopts a unique visual style that distinguishes it from the cel-shaded or photorealistic trends of the era.
The characters in Kururin Squash! are rendered as 2D flat artwork, but they exist within a fully 3D world.
The characters in Kururin Squash! move like paper puppets on sticks.
When a character turns or changes expression, the flat model flips over to reveal a different drawing on the reverse side.
This "cardboard cutout" aesthetic gives the cutscenes a charming, storybook quality.
While the gameplay plane is 2D, the environments in Kururin Squash! are fully polygonal 3D.
This depth is used for visual flair, such as seeing butterflies fluttering in a forest far below the glass floor of the maze, or enemies being launched into the foreground when defeated by a tornado.
The GameCube's hardware allowed for advanced lighting effects in Kururin Squash!.
Lasers cast halos of light, explosions generate particle clouds, and water surfaces have realistic transparency in Kururin Squash!.
These effects serve not just as eye candy but as visual feedback for the player's actions.
The audio landscape of Kururin Squash!, crafted by Atsuhiro Motoyama, is integral to the "flow" of the game.
The soundtrack of Kururin Squash! features upbeat, rhythmic electronic music that matches the constant rotation of the Helirin.

Sound effects in Kururin Squash! are punchy and distinct—the thwack of the boxing glove, the whoosh of the flamethrower, and the shattering glass sound of a destroyed Helirin provide immediate auditory feedback.
Despite its quality, Kururin Squash! was a commercial disappointment.
In its debut week (October 14, 2004), Kururin Squash! charted at #18 in Japan, selling only 5,745 copies.
Kururin Squash! quickly fell out of the charts, accumulating a total of approximately 18,562 copies sold by the end of 2004.
This performance made Kururin Squash! the lowest-selling entry in the Kururin series.

Furthermore, Kururin Squash! holds the dubious distinction of being the second lowest-selling first-party Nintendo title on the GameCube in Japan, outperforming only Eternal Darkness: Sanity's Requiem.
Several factors likely contributed to Kururin Squash!'s poor market performance.
By late 2004, the GameCube was struggling against the dominance of the PlayStation 2.
The audience that remained was often focused on major franchises (Zelda, Mario, Metroid) rather than experimental puzzle games.
The "irritating stick" genre (a reference to the Japanese game show segment Iraira Bou) is inherently niche.
While popular on handhelds for short bursts of play, it was a harder sell as a home console experience requiring dedicated TV time.
Kururin Squash! was never released in North America or Europe.
While the GBA title Kuru Kuru Kururin had a European release, the GameCube sequel Kururin Squash! remained Japan-exclusive.
This limited Kururin Squash!'s potential audience strictly to the Japanese market and a small community of importers.
In Japan, Kururin Squash! received respectable scores, though it was not hailed as a masterpiece.
The prestigious magazine Famitsu awarded Kururin Squash! a score of roughly 30/40 (averaging 7.5/10), with individual reviewers giving it scores of 8s and 7s.
Reviewers praised the polished mechanics and the transition to 3D but likely found the content volume or difficulty curve to be barriers to a higher score.
Interestingly, Western critics who imported Kururin Squash! often rated it higher than their Japanese counterparts, charmed by its unique mechanics and lack of language barrier.
Nintendo World Report awarded Kururin Squash! a stellar 9.5/10.
The reviewer called Kururin Squash! "excellent" and praised the "incredible graphic style" and "lastability," recommending it unreservedly to puzzle fans.
IGN provided a glowing playtest of Kururin Squash!, describing the experience as "addictive" and stating, "We can't stop playing this thing."
IGN highlighted the multiplayer mode of Kururin Squash! as a potential "riot" and urged Nintendo of America to localize it.
Eurogamer gave Kururin Squash! a 7/10, and Edge gave it a 6/10, reflecting a more critical view of its niche appeal and difficulty spikes.
A recurring theme in Western coverage is the accessibility of Kururin Squash!.
Despite being fully in Japanese, critics universally noted that the language barrier for Kururin Squash! was "zilch".
The menus were intuitive, and the gameplay communicated its goals through visual design alone.
This made Kururin Squash! a staple recommendation for GameCube owners looking to import Japanese exclusives.
Kururin Squash! leverages the GameCube's four-controller ports to offer robust local multiplayer.
Up to four players compete in split-screen to finish a stage first in Race Mode.
Race Mode emphasizes speed and risk management.
Players share a screen or arena in Battle Mode, using offensive Helirins (like the boxing or tornado types) to knock opponents into walls or hazards.
This chaotic mode was compared favorably to Super Monkey Ball's party games.
To enhance replayability, Kururin Squash! features a shop system run by the characters.
Coins collected in levels are used as currency in the shop.
Players can buy practical items like "Heart-Ups" (extra health) and "Amazing Hearts" (checkpoints), as well as cosmetic items like new Helirin colors from the shop.
The shop also sells unlockable minigames that can be downloaded to a Game Boy Advance via the GameCube-GBA Link Cable, a feature that rewarded cross-platform ownership.
Kururin Squash! effectively marked the end of the Kururin franchise.
No mainline sequel has been produced since 2004.
The commercial failure of Kururin Squash! likely signaled to Nintendo that the concept had reached its market ceiling.
While the GBA titles were re-released on the Wii U Virtual Console, Kururin Squash! remains trapped on the GameCube, never having seen a digital re-release.
Despite its dormancy, the Kururin series is acknowledged in Nintendo's crossover fighter, Super Smash Bros.
The Helirin appears as a trophy/spirit in Super Smash Bros.
The "Kururin" universe is cataloged in the game's archives, with Squash! noted as the most recent entry.
Today, Kururin Squash! is a collector's item.
Due to its low print run and Japan exclusivity, Kururin Squash! commands a premium price.
Complete copies (CIB) of Kururin Squash! sell for approximately $47.
Graded copies of Kururin Squash! can reach upwards of $146.

Kururin Squash! is sought after not just for its rarity, but for its status as a high-quality, "hidden gem" of the GameCube library that showcases Nintendo's willingness to experiment with weird, wonderful concepts.
Kururin Squash! is a game of contradictions.
Kururin Squash! is a visually vibrant, 3D console game that plays strictly in 2D.
Kururin Squash! is a critically acclaimed title that failed commercially.
Kururin Squash! is a "casual" puzzle game with a punishing difficulty curve.
These contradictions are precisely what make Kururin Squash! a fascinating subject of study.
Kururin Squash! represents the pinnacle of the Kururin formula—refined, expanded, and polished to a shine—before the series was quietly retired.
For those who played it, whether in Japan in 2004 or as importers years later, Kururin Squash! remains a "delightful" and "addictive" testament to the creative spirit of the GameCube era.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

| Kururin Squash! |
| --- |
| [![Image 2: Kururin Squash! game cover shows the character riding on a rotating pole through a whimsical landscape of candy trees, floating platforms, and rainbow bridges](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/4/45/Kururin_Squash_GameCube_box_art.png/250px-Kururin_Squash_GameCube_box_art.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kururin_Squash_GameCube_box_art.png) |
| [Developer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_developer "Video game developer") | [Eighting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eighting "Eighting") |
| [Publisher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_publisher "Video game publisher") | [Nintendo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo "Nintendo") |
| [Directors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_creative_director "Video game creative director") | Shinji Hatano Tomonori Fujisawa |
| [Producers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_producer "Video game producer") | Hiroshi Sato Masato Toyoshima |
| [Artists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_artist "Video game artist") | Nanako Kinoshita Tomomi Sano Ryuusuke Yoshida Takayoshi Matsui |
| [Composer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_composer "Video game composer") | Atsuhiro Motoyama |
| Series | _Kururin_ |
| [Platform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computing_platform "Computing platform") | [GameCube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube "GameCube") |
| Release | * [JP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan"): October 14, 2004[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-release-1) |
| [Genres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_genre "Video game genre") | [Puzzle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puzzle_video_game "Puzzle video game"), [action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_game "Action game") |
| Modes | [Single-player](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single-player "Single-player"), [multiplayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplayer "Multiplayer") |

_**Kururin Squash!**_[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-2) is a 2004 [puzzle video game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puzzle_video_game "Puzzle video game") developed by [Eighting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eighting "Eighting") and published by [Nintendo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo "Nintendo") for the [GameCube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube "GameCube"). It was released exclusively in Japan on October 14, 2004. _Kururin Squash!_ is the third and final game in the _Kururin_ series as well as the first entry on a home console, following the release of _[Kuru Kuru Kururin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuru\_Kuru\_Kururin "Kuru Kuru Kururin")_ (2001) and _[Kururin Paradise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin\_Paradise "Kururin Paradise")_ (2002) on the [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance"). The game uses [3D graphics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3D_computer_graphics "3D computer graphics"), with 2D artwork of its characters being used on cardboard cutouts outside of gameplay.

_Kururin Squash!_ is a maze navigation game where the player attempts to reach the goal at the end for a high score. It introduces coins, enemies, and bosses in its levels, with multiple new vehicles being used to overcome specific obstacles. _Kururin Squash!_ received generally positive reviews from critics for its gameplay, visuals, and style, with mixed opinions on its difficulty. It is considered to be one of the best Japanese-exclusive GameCube games. Selling less than 20,000 copies, it is the lowest-selling _Kururin_ game, and it is Nintendo's second worst-performing GameCube game in Japan.

[![Image 3: This screenshot shows the Helibokaan flying in a circular arena, attacking the barrier protecting Professor Isogashima. The game's interface displays the time, coin counter score, and Kururin with all three of his hearts remaining.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/1/17/Kururin_Squash_Boss_Fight_Screenshot.jpg/250px-Kururin_Squash_Boss_Fight_Screenshot.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kururin_Squash_Boss_Fight_Screenshot.jpg)

Kururin piloting the Helibokaan during the [boss fight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boss_(video_games) "Boss (video games)") against Professor Isogashima in the first world.

The player controls Kururin, a bird who pilots the Helirin, a constantly spinning helicopter, by navigating [mazes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maze "Maze") while avoiding walls and other obstacles. The player can hold down buttons on the [GameCube controller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube_controller "GameCube controller") to adjust the speed at which the Helirin spins and the speed of the Helirin itself.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-HardcoreGaming101-3) Kururin has three hearts by default, and each stage contains checkpoints where their hearts can be refilled.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-NWR-4) If the player hits any obstacles, they lose a heart, and three seconds are added to the in-game timer, with the goal being to complete each stage in the least amount of time for a high score.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Manual-5) In the single-player mode, the player can select whether to control a larger or more compact Helirin, a method of adjusting difficulty.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-:0-6) Two modes are available from the start, the Adventure mode with the stages and story, as well as a Challenge mode where the player attempts to complete the stages as fast as possible.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Edge-7) After completing the Adventure mode, a third mode is unlocked where the player controls the center sphere of the Helirin, which does not feature the rotating helicopter blades, but can't stop moving.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-8) After completing this mode, the Extra mode is unlocked, featuring rotated versions of the stages.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-9)

_Kururin Squash!_ introduces new vehicles, enemies in stages, and [boss fights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boss_(video_games) "Boss (video games)") at the end of each world. The "Action Helirins" are helicopters that provide various advantages the standard Helirin does not. One of these vehicles is the Helibokaan,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-10) which is a helicopter that can break obstacles and punch enemies. The Helibashan can dive underwater to avoid obstacles on the surface, the Heliboboh can shoot fire when attached to rails, the Heliburuun can create whirlwinds, and the Helibibyuun can shoot objects using rapid fire.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-11)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Manual-5): 12–13  The single-player modes feature several unique worlds, with every few stages taking place in a new environment.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Nintendojo-12)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Manual-5): 28–29  Coins are present in every stage, and collecting all the coins will net the player a perfect bonus, increasing their total coin counter.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Euro-13) Coins can be used in shops, which contain many useful items and accessories. These items can increase the player's hearts, respawn them at the beginning after they lose their hearts, or provide a minimap for stages. The shop also contains movies that can guide the player on how to complete individual levels,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-HardcoreGaming101-3) with shops being run by members of the Magic Group, the false antagonists from _[Kururin Paradise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin\_Paradise "Kururin Paradise")_.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-NWR-4)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Manual-5): 21

The multiplayer in _Kururin Squash!_ has two modes that support up to four players. The Race Mode has over forty obstacle courses where players attempt to reach the end while hitting opponents into walls or blocking their opponents' vehicles, taking place on stages from the Challenge mode.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Nintendojo-12) In the Battle Mode, players can fight on ten unique stages by using power-ups and weapons that is similar to [minigames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minigame "Minigame") from [_Super Monkey Ball_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Monkey_Ball_(video_game) "Super Monkey Ball (video game)").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Nintendojo-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Cult_Classics-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Kikizo-15) The objective for this mode is to collect the most coins while attacking other players.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-NWR-4) By connecting a [GameCube – Game Boy Advance link cable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube_%E2%80%93_Game_Boy_Advance_link_cable "GameCube – Game Boy Advance link cable"), up to four [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance") systems can play a [spot the difference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spot_the_difference "Spot the difference")-type quiz game, which can be purchased from the shop.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Kikizo-15)

[![Image 4: This screenshot depicts the ending cutscene for the first world, with Kururin rescuing his youngest siblings, Hyokorin and Loverin, from Professor Isogashima. The characters are illustrated on cardboard cutouts, which are held up by sticks extending to the bottom of the screen.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/3/3d/Kururin_Squash%21_Cutscene_Screenshot.png/250px-Kururin_Squash%21_Cutscene_Screenshot.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kururin_Squash!_Cutscene_Screenshot.png)

The story is told through a [paper puppet theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toy_theater "Toy theater") style, which received praise from critics.

After Kururin wins the lottery for his family, they travel across the four continents of the world. However, upon arriving back to their home in Kururin Village, only the parents of the family return. After losing track of his family members, Kururin goes on an adventure to find them across the four continents.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-:0-6)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Manual-5): 6–7  Throughout the journey, Kururin's guide, Teacher Hare, provides him with new Action Helirins that help him progress through the different worlds.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Manual-5): 12–13  Kururin travels to face Professor Isogashima, a mad inventor bird who has captured all the members of his family since they interfered with his research, and he releases them after being defeated in boss battles.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-:0-6)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-16) Professor Isogashima and his Isogashimachines serve as the main antagonists with the goal of making everyone else busy.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-17) Once Kururin returns home after rescuing his siblings, he discovers that his parents were also kidnapped by Professor Isogashima, so he travels to the fifth and final world in space to rescue them.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-18) When defeated, Professor Isogashima crash lands on their home planet, makes himself busy by fixing the problems caused by his Isogashimachines, and the Kururin family returns home.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-19)

_Kururin Squash!_ was developed by [Eighting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eighting "Eighting"), and was the first game in the _Kururin_ series to transition from 2D to [3D computer graphics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3D_computer_graphics "3D computer graphics"). The directors and producers from _[Kururin Paradise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin\_Paradise "Kururin Paradise")_ returned to work on _Kururin Squash!_ as the final entry in the series. [Yōichi Kotabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Y%C5%8Dichi_Kotabe "Yōichi Kotabe") returns as the series' character designer, with it being the final game he serves that role at Nintendo prior to his departure from the company in 2007.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Credits-20) It was officially revealed in an issue of _[Famitsu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Famitsu "Famitsu")_ magazine on August 5, 2004,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-21) and later released on October 14, 2004. It had a small advertising campaign, with a publication in a column of _[Nintendo Dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo\_Dream "Nintendo Dream")_ and commercials that used the Helirin as a prop.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-23) In a developer interview with [Yuichi Toyama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuichi_Toyama "Yuichi Toyama") and Kenichi Yokoo for _[Sōkyūgurentai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terra\_Diver "Terra Diver")_ and _[Mahou Daisakusen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sorcer\_Striker "Sorcer Striker")_, Yokoo cited _Kururin Squash!_ as his favorite non-arcade game he worked on.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-24) Eighting would later collaborate with Nintendo on the [Nintendo DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS "Nintendo DS") game _[Master of Illusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master\_of\_Illusion\_(video\_game) "Master of Illusion (video game)")_ in 2006.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-25)

_Kururin Squash!_ received generally positive reviews,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-GameStats-31) with praise for the 3D visuals,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-NWR-4)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Cult_Classics-14) music,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-NWR-4)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Kikizo-15)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Nintendojo-12) as well as improved gameplay and controls from its predecessors.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Nintendojo-12)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-:0-6) The art style received praise, with colorful 3D environments and stylized cutscenes represented by cardboard puppets on sticks, creating a unique and refreshing style.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-NWRPrev-32)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-NWR-4)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Kikizo-15)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Nintendojo-12) The multiplayer modes were also complimented for their quality. Caleb Gossler of _Nintendojo_ claimed _Kururin Squash!_ to have "some of the best four-player party games on the GameCube".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Nintendojo-12) Chandra Nair of _[GamesTM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GamesTM "GamesTM")_ described the levels as "cunningly designed", complimenting them for taking advantage of the different abilities of the Action Helirins.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-GTM-27) Ben Kosmina of _Nintendo World Report_ described the overall experience as stellar, complimenting the title for having a low language barrier to enjoy the gameplay, despite its exclusivity to Japan.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-NWR-4) Similarly, Nadia Grace Mullings of _Game Rant_ claimed it to be "worthy of being one of the best GameCube titles, despite it having never been released in America".[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-:1-33) Anoop Gantayat of _[IGN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGN "IGN")_ expressed interest in _Kururin Squash!_ releasing overseas due to the addictive gameplay, even if there were no plans to do so by [Nintendo of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_of_America "Nintendo of America").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-:0-6) The low price was also praised, with _[Edge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edge\_(magazine) "Edge (magazine)")_ magazine describing the price point as enticing.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-34)

The main criticism of _Kururin Squash!_ was its difficulty and short length. In comparison to the Game Boy Advance titles which featured more challenging stages, _Kururin Squash!_ contains generally easier levels that could be completed faster due to the improvement in movement accuracy, as a result of switching from a [d-pad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D-pad "D-pad") to the GameCube control stick.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-HardcoreGaming101-3)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-GTM-Mag-26)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Euro-13)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Edge-7) Despite this critique, others have claimed the difficulty level is still present. Jonti Davies of _Kikizo_ described the gameplay as "straightforward in principle, but, in later stages especially, often devilishly difficult in practice".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Kikizo-15) Ollie Reynolds of _Nintendo Life_ shared this sentiment, noting how navigating the mazes can become "incredibly tense" as the player progresses.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-:2-35)_[Eurogamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurogamer "Eurogamer")_ later retracted this criticism, with Keza MacDonald stating that it hardly affects the overall experience, considering _Kururin Squash!_ a [cult classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult_video_game "Cult video game") on the GameCube.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Cult_Classics-14) Additionally, critics were disappointed by the lack of multiplayer modes, in comparison to the multiple [minigames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minigame "Minigame") introduced in _Kururin Paradise_. Ben Kosmina of _Nintendo World Report_ considered the fewer number of multiplayer offerings disappointing.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-NWRPrev-32) Writers for _Edge_ magazine claimed the sixteen minigames from _Kururin Paradise_ were better than having only two in _Kururin Squash!_, with the Game Boy Advance link cable minigame being referred to as "no more than a novelty".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Edge-7) In retrospective reviews, _Kururin Squash!_ has been cited as one of the best Japanese-exclusive GameCube games,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-:1-33)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-36)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-37)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Cult_Classics-14) with many desiring an English localization.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-38)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-:2-35)

In Japan, _Kururin Squash!_ reached the eighteenth position on sales charts during its initial launch week, selling 5,745 copies.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-39) It only placed among the top thirty weekly video game sales one additional time the following week.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-40)_Kururin Squash!_ sold a total of 18,562 copies in Japan from release to December 20, 2004.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-41) It was the third lowest-selling GameCube game in 2004 and the second lowest-selling first-party game behind [_Eternal Darkness: Sanity's Requiem_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eternal_Darkness "Eternal Darkness"),[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-42) subsequently making it the lowest-selling entry in the _Kururin_ series, despite being sold at a budget price comparative to other GameCube titles.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-release-1)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-43)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-44)

We are constantly working to enhance the user experience for both contributors and readers, improve site security, and ensure reliable access to our websites globally. This infrastructure and product support sustain one of the top ten most visited websites in the world, all at a fraction of the cost of popular for-profit websites.

_**Kuru Kuru Kururin**_[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuru_Kuru_Kururin#cite_note-1) is a [puzzle video game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puzzle_video_game "Puzzle video game") developed by [Eighting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eighting "Eighting") and published by [Nintendo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo "Nintendo") for the [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance") (GBA). It was released in Japan on March 21, 2001, and in Europe and Australia on June 22 as a launch title. It was not released in North America until February 2016 via the [Wii U](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_U "Wii U")'s [Virtual Console](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_Console "Virtual Console") service. _Kuru Kuru Kururin_ is the first title in the _Kururin_ series and was followed by two Japan-only sequels, _[Kururin Paradise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin\_Paradise "Kururin Paradise")_ and _[Kururin Squash!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin\_Squash! "Kururin Squash!")_. The game was released on the [Nintendo Classics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Classics "Nintendo Classics") service in February 2023.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuru_Kuru_Kururin#cite_note-2)

Gameplay
--------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kuru_Kuru_Kururin&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Gameplay")]

[![Image 12: A screenshot from a video game shows the character in the bottom left and a counter at the top left, a horizontal passage with a rotating cylinder in the center, and a colorful circular design at the right](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/8/89/Kurukurukururin_screenshot.PNG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kurukurukururin_screenshot.PNG)

Screenshot of _Kuru Kuru Kururin_

The player controls a slowly spinning stick, and must maneuver it through a series of [mazes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maze "Maze") without touching the walls. Infamously difficult,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuru_Kuru_Kururin#cite_note-3) the single player offers several goals per course, while the 4 player (single cart) multiplayer pits players in a race for fastest clear times.

The game starts with simple training levels, in which players are told how to play and how to get around the first corners. After that, there are three levels in each stage, which get progressively harder and longer. The obstacles and the look of the levels (ice, cave, machine, etc.) vary between stages. Taking damage incurs a time penalty, and losing all lives results in failing the level, requiring the player to restart the level from the beginning. Beginners can play the levels on Easy mode, where the stick is only half of its usual size.

There is a mode called Challenge mode, which is a collection of smaller levels, usually involving only one or two corners or objects to dodge.

Plot
----

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kuru_Kuru_Kururin&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Plot")]

The story begins when Kururin's brothers and sisters go missing, and it is up to him to find them. Kururin is initially unsure that he is up to the task because he has never left his home world before. Being the adventurous and helpful fellow he is, Kururin agrees to rescue his lost family. Teacher Hare trains Kururin in the art of controlling the Helirin, a stick-shaped helicopter that has a slow-spinning propeller. Piloting the Helirin through the different worlds will be a difficult task, but using Teacher Hare's valuable lessons, Kururin bravely sets out on his adventure to rescue his lost family.

Development
-----------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kuru_Kuru_Kururin&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Development")]

_Kuru Kuru Kururin_ was developed by the Japanese company [Eighting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eighting "Eighting") and first announced at the [Nintendo Space World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Space_World "Nintendo Space World") 2000.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuru_Kuru_Kururin#cite_note-4)

Reception
---------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kuru_Kuru_Kururin&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Reception")]

Reception

Review scores| Publication | Score |
| --- | --- |
| _[Computer and Video Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer\_and\_Video\_Games "Computer and Video Games")_ | 5/10 |
| _[Edge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edge\_(magazine) "Edge (magazine)")_ | 7/10[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuru_Kuru_Kururin#cite_note-5) |
| _[Eurogamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurogamer "Eurogamer")_ | 9/10[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuru_Kuru_Kururin#cite_note-6) |
| _[GameSpot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameSpot "GameSpot")_ | 7.1/10 |
| _Nintendo World Report_ | 9/10 |

_Kuru Kuru Kururin_ received mostly positive reviews from critics. It was praised for its simple yet addictive gameplay. [Eurogamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurogamer "Eurogamer") rated the game a score of 9 out of 10 points. The reviewer lauded the game's learning curve and stated that there would be no other puzzle game on the Game Boy Advance at the time that can "rival _Kuru Kuru Kururin_ for its sheer addictiveness and fun-value".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuru_Kuru_Kururin#cite_note-7) Nintendo World Report, then known as Planet GameCube, gave _Kuru Kuru Kururin_ the same score as Eurogamer and declared that it is "simple enough that anyone can pick this game up and play". The reviewer praised the game's multiplayer mode, which he described as "an absolute blast", as well as its lasting appeal, but also commented that the "cutesy" characters and music would be a turn-off for "a lot of people".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuru_Kuru_Kururin#cite_note-8)[Jeff Gerstmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Gerstmann "Jeff Gerstmann") of [GameSpot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameSpot "GameSpot") rated _Kuru Kuru Kururin_ 7.1 out of 10 and described its graphics as "simple but effective". He stated that the game is "excellent at filling up small periods of free time with its short, level-based nature".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuru_Kuru_Kururin#cite_note-9)_[Computer and Video Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer\_and\_Video\_Games "Computer and Video Games")_ was less impressed by the game, rating it 5 out of 10. The reviewer declared the game to be "extremely frustrating" and said that it lacks "the perfect simplicity" of other puzzle games such as _[Mr. Driller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr.\_Driller "Mr. Driller")_ and _[Tetris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetris "Tetris")_. Nonetheless, he also commented that the novel gameplay of _Kuru Kuru Kururin_ "will find many fans" and that the multiplayer mode is "unexpectedly brilliant".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuru_Kuru_Kururin#cite_note-10)

Legacy
------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kuru_Kuru_Kururin&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Legacy")]

The first sequel, _Kururin Paradise_, was released in 2002 for the Game Boy Advance. It was released in Japan only, even though _Kururin Paradise_ was previously showcased at [E3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_Entertainment_Expo "Electronic Entertainment Expo")[2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_E3#2002 "History of E3"), the first time a _Kururin_ game had been announced for the American market.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuru_Kuru_Kururin#cite_note-11) Another sequel was also released only in Japan for the [GameCube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube "GameCube") in 2004, entitled _[Kururin Squash!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin\_Squash! "Kururin Squash!")_, which became the only title of the series to use [3D computer graphics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3D_computer_graphics "3D computer graphics"), as well as to appear on a home console.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuru_Kuru_Kururin#cite_note-12)

Several references to the _Kururin_ series are made in the [_Super Smash Bros._ series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Smash_Bros._(series) "Super Smash Bros. (series)"). The Helirin makes a cameo appearance as a trophy in _[Melee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super\_Smash\_Bros.\_Melee "Super Smash Bros. Melee")_, but is incorrectly referred to as "Heririn" in the American version. The Helirin later appears in _[Brawl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super\_Smash\_Bros.\_Brawl "Super Smash Bros. Brawl")_ as an Assist Trophy. Unlike most Assist Trophies, it doesn't attack, but it becomes part of the stage, and can be used as a platform or a wall.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuru_Kuru_Kururin#cite_note-13) Several other things in the _Kururin_ series appear as Trophies and Stickers in the game.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuru_Kuru_Kururin#cite_note-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuru_Kuru_Kururin#cite_note-15)

9.content:
_**This page contains story spoilers.**_

_Kururin Squash!_ is the third and final game in the Kururin series. It was released for the [GameCube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube) on October 14th, 2004. Unlike its predecessors, _Kururin Squash!_ has never been rereleased, and remains exclusive to the GameCube.

[![Image 1](https://static.wikitide.net/kururinwiki/f/f4/Kururin_Squash%21_Coverart.jpg)](https://kururin.miraheze.org/wiki/File:Kururin_Squash!_Coverart.jpg)

Coverart of Kururin Squash!

The story follows [Kururin](https://kururin.miraheze.org/wiki/Kururin "Kururin"), who was on a free family vacation his family won. However, when Kururin gets home, he notices all his siblings are gone. Professor Isogashima had captured them, and he built several robots to stop Kururin from "interfering with his research". After Kururin rescues all his siblings, he goes home, but his father, Totorin, is not there. Isogashima had kidnapped him in Wonderverse, the final level in the game. So Kururin rides the [Helirin](https://kururin.miraheze.org/wiki/Helirin "Helirin") to save him. Beatable "Dad" times on each level are unlocked after rescuing Totorin. Throughout the game, Teacher Hare invents new Helirins to help Kururin progress.

[![Image 2](https://static.wikitide.net/kururinwiki/thumb/c/c1/Why_are_you_catching_my_brothers%3F.png/300px-Why_are_you_catching_my_brothers%3F.png)](https://kururin.miraheze.org/wiki/File:Why_are_you_catching_my_brothers%3F.png)

A screenshot of the first cutscene of the NewGBAXL English translation patch of Kururin Squash!

The gameplay is similar to the prior 2 games. You control the [Helirin](https://kururin.miraheze.org/wiki/Helirin "Helirin"), an automatically spinning stick, through tight mazes. When Helirin hits the wall, you lose a heart. When you lose all 3 (5 if a Heart-Up is used) hearts, Helirin shatters and the level must be restarted, or, if an Amazing Heart is used, restart from the last heart panel. By pressing the B button, Helirin will move faster and by pressing the R button, Helirin will rotate faster. There are blue springs throughout the levels that will cause Helirin to rotate in the opposite direction it's currently rotating in. New to this game, are five Helirins, [Helibokaan](https://kururin.miraheze.org/wiki/Helibokaan "Helibokaan"), [Helibashan](https://kururin.miraheze.org/wiki/Helibashan "Helibashan"), [Heliboboh](https://kururin.miraheze.org/wiki/Heliboboh "Heliboboh"), [Heliburuun](https://kururin.miraheze.org/wiki/Heliburuun "Heliburuun"), and [Helibibyuun](https://kururin.miraheze.org/wiki/Helibibyuun "Helibibyuun"). The Helibokaan (Helibash in the NewGBAXL patch) is used in some levels in Sweet Shores. When the A button is pressed, the boxing gloves on both end of it will extend, and it will punch through obstacles and enemies, rewarding the player with coins. The Helibashan (Helibubble in the NewGBAXL patch) is used in some levels in Coastal Canopy. When the A button is pressed, Helibashan will go underwater until either the A button is released, or when air runs out. The Heliboboh (Heliblaze in the NewGBAXL patch) is used in some levels in Snowscape. When the A button is pressed, flames will released from either side, which will kill enemies. If you dash with the B button, the flames get longer. The Heliburuun (Heliblow in the NewGBAXL patch) is used in some levels in CyberCity. If you hold the A button long enough, when you let go, a tornado will be released that can kill enemies, reveal areas obscured by smoke, and block fire. The Helibibyuun (Helibeam in the NewGBAXL patch) is used in some levels in Wonderverse. When the A button is pressed, lasers will shoot out of either side of it. These lasers kill enemies and can shoot bombs. At the end of each world, you fight a boss with the Helirin used in that level.

[![Image 3](https://static.wikitide.net/kururinwiki/thumb/2/22/Sweet_Shores_4_Screenshot.png/300px-Sweet_Shores_4_Screenshot.png)](https://kururin.miraheze.org/wiki/File:Sweet_Shores_4_Screenshot.png)

A screenshot of the level Sweet Shores 4.

7.title: Kururin Squash! Review - Review
7.content:
Kuru Kuru Kururin debuted for both the Japanese and European Game Boy Advance launches. The idea was deceptively simple -- all you have to do was guide a constantly rotating stick through a maze and reach the goal without hitting any obstacles. Doing so makes you lose time and health. Three hits and you have to start again. Kururin Squash is the third game in the series, and as such, it expands on this basic idea of navigating your way through a maze. In addition to the standard helicopter, you're now able to guide specially designed helicopters that allow you to punch, dive, shoot flames and throw tornados.

As mentioned in my [impressions](http://www.planetgamecube.com/impressions.cfm?action=profile&id=716), the first thing that will strike you about the game is the incredible graphic style. (Take a look at the intro, which is available for [download](http://www.planetgamecube.com/news.cfm?action=item&id=5745) to see for yourself.) The graphics are crisp and bright, and all the characters in cutscenes are moved around as though they were puppets on sticks, with additional sticks used for controlling their arms. If they want to change expressions, the character will flip around and a completely different version of the same character will be on the other side. It's a really refreshing look, and I've never seen anything like it before.

The levels themselves are fully polygonal, which is a massive leap from the 2D (but still excellent) sprite graphics of the previous games. The mazes have some great transparency effects that allow you to see, for example, forests with butterflies underneath you. Other high points for the GameCube version are the lighting and particle effects. It's quite strange to see such great effects in a puzzle game, but there they are. Dust will kick up when you punch walls, lasers will leave light halos, and there are surprisingly massive explosions for destroying enemies. Enemies caught in tornados will be spun high in the air and fly right towards the camera. The effects are subtle, but very pretty.

The game's soundtrack is quite decent. Although the music tracks clock in at around a minute before they begin to loop, they're pleasant enough for you not to notice. There're a large variety of instruments used, including a very Seventies-like "wikky-wa" guitar melody when you successfully complete a level. Each level's music suits its area - the sky levels have airy, futuristic music, the ocean level music is wonderfully mellow, and the boss theme is suitably frantic. Most of the sound effects are strikingly similar to the Game Boy Advance games, which is not a problem, as it keeps a sense of familiarity. Most other sounds are similar to typical video-game sounds, but it's wonderfully satisfying to hear the "whoosh" of the flamethrower Heririn (or helicopter). The only problem that I have with the game's sound are the noises used for the character speech. It's a kind of high-pitched tweeting, and because I use headphones a lot, it rattles right through my brain.

Kururin Squash mixes elements from the previous games -- that is, the guiding of a constantly rotating stick through a maze without hitting anything -- and adds new helicopters that cause the player to think a bit more carefully when guiding them. The Punch Heririn can be used to destroy obstacles and enemies, but you get a bit of recoil from it, so you need to allow a little leeway when you use it. The Dive Heririn will cause you to think on two different levels, as you'll have to play through sections of levels which need to be quickly navigated by rising and submerging again, in some cases fighting strong currents and whirlpools. The Flame Heririn makes things incredibly tough, as the levels take place entirely on-rails. Using the Control Stick will freely rotate the Heririn, and you'll occasionally need to dodge precariously placed crystals and massive enemies that chase you throughout the level. The Tornado Heririn also allows for some clever puzzles. Some will see you temporarily blocking an enemy dispenser; others will have you safely riding in a tornado as you launch it down a corridor full of flamethrowers. You'll also need to learn to use those special Heririns for clever boss battles. Eighting have gone all-out in using the GameCube to create an expanded Kururin experience.

Kururin Squash is also the first game in the series to introduce currency. Strewn throughout the stages are gold coins -- collect all of them in a stage in addition to not getting hurt at all and you'll earn yourself a perfect clear. Coins can also be earned by defeating enemies. You won't need to collect those, as they'll be collected automatically. Coins can be used in the various shops on the map screen (the Carnies from Kururin Paradise make cameo appearances in running the shops), where you'll be able to purchase various items. They include world maps, a GBA to GC Link Up Mini-Game, additional Heririns, Customizable HUDs, and Teacher Hare Movies that show you how to beat the stages safely. Some of the Heririns include a Chocolate Bar, a Tank, and a Heririn with Nintendo logo blades that plays the Super Mario Bros. coin sound when you press the horn. Collecting all of the shop items is purely optional, but it makes for a good reason to return to the game.

The Battle Multiplayer in Squash definitely seems to be more fun than the Race Mode. In Race, avid Kururin players have a distinct advantage over novices, whereas with Battle it's all about beating each other up, powering up, and collecting the most coins. The tables can quickly turn if you have the right power up. In Race, although the leader gets a handicap of becoming larger, they can easily overcome this if they're a skilled player. The GBA to GC link-up game is basically just a memory match game, which is a bit of a shame.

The biggest injustice is that this will be the third Kururin game to not see the light of day outside of Japan. It's totally bizarre as to why, as the game represents everything that Nintendo could possibly want -- a simple, yet fun concept, a new franchise, and a game that can be played without having to worry about the language barrier. If you like your puzzle games and have not heard of the Kururin series before, I'd **highly** recommend getting this game. Actually, I'd recommend all three, as they're all stellar games. Kururin Squash continues the series' legacy of great fun, lastability, and typical Japanese wackiness. As an import game, the language barrier is zilch. Pick it up from our partners at [Lik-Sang](http://www.lik-sang.com/info.php?category=79&products_id=5407&) now!

Kururin Squash!
===============

Posted by [Kurt Kalata](http://www.hardcoregaming101.net/author/kurt/)on May 18, 2010

![Image 6: Game screenshot of Super Monkey Ball Adventure features a colorful and psychedelic environment with a timer at the top left and a health bar on the left side](http://www.hardcoregaming101.net/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/squash-07.png)

#### Kururin Squash! (くるりんスカッシュ!) - GameCube (October 14, 2004)

This entry is part 3 of 3 in the series [Kuru Kuru Kururin](http://www.hardcoregaming101.net/series/kuru-kuru-kururin/ "Kuru Kuru Kururin")

[Kuru Kuru Kururin](http://www.hardcoregaming101.net/series/kuru-kuru-kururin/ "Kuru Kuru Kururin")

*   [Kuru Kuru Kururin](http://www.hardcoregaming101.net/kuru-kuru-kururin/ "Kuru Kuru Kururin")
*   [Kururin Paradise](http://www.hardcoregaming101.net/kururin-paradise/ "Kururin Paradise")
*   Kururin Squash!

[![Image 8: Kururin Squash! Japanese Nintendo Gamecube box art shows the protagonist in a large plane moving along a whimsical track that weaves around candy colored structures](http://www.hardcoregaming101.net/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/squash-259x360.jpg)](http://www.hardcoregaming101.net/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/squash.jpg)

Kururin’s only console installment utilizes 3D graphics while keeping the same 2D mechanics. The visuals aren’t technically all that impressive (cel shaded polygons similar to the style of _Kururin Paradise_ would have been nicer), but they’re colorful and still plenty attractive. In the cutscenes, Kururin and pals are rendered as little cardboard puppets held on sticks, making for some pretty amusing cutscenes reminiscent of a kid’s TV show. Beyond the graphics, the real advantage of being on a TV screen is that the field of vision is much wider, and the view isn’t nearly as cramped as it was in the GBA games. Although it doesn’t utilize true analog control (you still need to press B to speed up), the GameCube controller is much smoother than the GBA directional pad.

[![Image 10: Gameplay of Super Monkey Ball Adventure, in which the player character is in a jungle area, on a long path of yellow and orange color scheme, where he will pass through an arch-like formation with a pineapple underneath](http://www.hardcoregaming101.net/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/squash-02-480x360.png)](http://www.hardcoregaming101.net/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/squash-02.png)

While the alternate paths from _Kururin Paradise_ have been removed, each stage is now littered with coins. In order to get a perfect rating on a stage, you need to collect all coins in addition to reaching the exit without getting hit. Naturally, the stages can get pretty big, and you’ll need to cover every precarious nook and cranny to get 100%. You can also use these coins to buy a variety of items. Like the original, there are lots of useless things, like different Helirin skins or the ability to customize your life meter, but you can also buy maps, extra hearts, and an item that lets you continue from a checkpoint if you lose. There are also tons of super play videos to purchase.

In addition to the standard Helirin, there are now several different kinds of ships. One Helirin has boxing gloves at each end to knock around foes. Another has a pair of lasers. One can twirl around and shoot out miniature hurricanes, which can be used to push objects or block flame jets. Another lets you dive underwater, challenging you to dodge objects both above and below the surface. Most of these play similarly to the regular stages, but there’s also one where Helirin rides on a rail and can shoot flames out of its rotating blades. In addition to these new ships, there are still plenty of stages in the classic style. At the end of each world, you need to fight a boss battle using one of these new Helirins, challenging you at the skills you’ve learned throughout each zone. Including these boss levels, there are a total of forty stages in the Adventure mode of _Kururin Squash_. With the ability to use the items, most of these are quite easy, especially compared to _Kururin Paradise_. There are once again plenty of Challenge levels, but these are pretty short, as always. The multiplayer options are limited to a Race mode (similar to the first game) and a Battle mode, where up to four people beat each other up for coins. There’s also a Game Boy Advance mini game that can be played with the GBA link cable, but it’s a pretty crappy matching game.

[![Image 12: Video game screenshot depicting a character navigating a water course with obstacles like floating logs and spiky balls, set against a backdrop of a floral patterned path](http://www.hardcoregaming101.net/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/squash-08-480x360.png)](http://www.hardcoregaming101.net/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/squash-08.png)

Once again,_Kururin Squash_ stayed in Japan, although it’s quite cheap and easy to obtain. Just beware that playing on a non-Japanese GameCube with a Freeloader will cause most of the text to become garbled. Navigating menus is easy, but all of the plot scenes and item descriptions will be unreadable.
