11.title: Kururin Squash
11.description: Kururin Squash Balancing difficulty with fun can be a challenge in and of itself. An easy game can be enjoyed by players of any skill level, but it’s easy to look back on it and wish it could’ve …
11.content:
[![Image 1: Kat Koller](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:32:32/1*ecTfLFSdLD0GToo32qqb2A.png)](https://medium.com/@katcolonel?source=post_page---byline--6953298ee61d---------------------------------------)

8 min read

Feb 22, 2019

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![Image 2: Kurukuru Squash is displayed as a game title logo with a vibrant tropical background](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*7E1C0-g2_-ICpIYS4_6YPg.png)

Balancing difficulty with fun can be a challenge in and of itself. An easy game can be enjoyed by players of any skill level, but it’s easy to look back on it and wish it could’ve been a bit more; a hard game can either feel extremely satisfying to beat, or put up a huge wall that some people will get exhausted of slamming their heads against. But what makes a game hard? Is it swarms of merciless enemies unceasingly firing on a single, helpless player? Is it high-intensity one-on-one combat? Is it platforming where if you simply take one hit, you die?

Well, if Kururin has anything to say about it, it’s mostly claustrophobia.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![Image 3: Screenshot of a Klonoa 2: Lunatea's Veil video game level with Klonoa in the lower-left corner](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*a2ObXYkk4OzaRxYaqjdbZw.png)

Released in 2004 by Eighting, (formerly Eighting/Raizing, creators of Battle Garegga and Armed Police Batrider,) Kururin Squash is the third game in the Kururin trilogy. I’ll skip talking about the first two games because I can summarize my thoughts as, they’re good, but they don’t have much on Squash.

The core design of Kururin is simple: You control a flying machine with revolving wings, and you have to fly through mazes without slamming into walls or obstacles. Frequently, you’ll find blue springs that reverse your rotation so you can squeeze through different gaps. Kururin Squash doesn’t deviate from this core design, and by far I’d say it’s the best execution of it I’ve seen, well, ever.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![Image 4: Vivid and colorful 3D digital art features cartoon ducks in a game setting, surrounded by metallic structures, geometric patterns, and various game elements](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*P_SQrOxl9CIG5wJ4TTJUBg.png)

Kururin Squash’s success lies in its level design, which is easily the strongest of the series barring maybe some of the stages in Paradise. Most of the levels are the same basic gameplay as always, but with more screen space and tighter movement, managing yourself is a lot easier. You can see further ahead, and just have an easier time stopping before you smack your head against something. Even towards the end of the game, when it starts throwing some seriously tight curved pathways at you that you have to snake through, it never feels impossible, just really tense.

What’s maybe more notable about Squash, though, is its fresh inclusion of gimmick levels that totally shake up the basic design of the game, without losing the core focus.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![Image 5: Gameplay shot of Super Monkey Ball: Banana Blitz](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*Zc_lWOA_d8aJ2PEZsn_BEA.png)

Largely, these levels are actually extremely successful at what they set out to do, partially thanks to just the sheer variety of gimmicks on display. Every world has its own gimmick, every gimmick emphasizes something different, and no world has more than three of these levels. The result is something genuinely good at breaking the pace of the regular game that never overstays its welcome.

The gimmicks at play at their simplest revolve around punching enemies with boxing gloves and blasting them down with lasers, but the most interesting to me are world 2’s submarine stages that task you with raising and lowering between two layers to avoid hitting obstacles and to turn switches, world 3’s flamethrower stages that put you on rails and make you rotate to aim at enemies along the track while also spinning to avoid slamming into large crystals, and world 4’s propeller stages where your wings can be sped up fast enough to create gusts of air that can protect you from flames and launch away enemies.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![Image 6: A snapshot from the video game, Billy Hatcher and the Giant Egg, featuring a character with the timer in the upper-left corner and the race track around](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*cw5eeJW7Lo8zVFmjSJ_VIA.png)

All three of these gimmicks either build on the foundation of Kururin, or add a twist so unique and satisfying that it almost feels like a different game. I wouldn’t want Squash to focus purely on any of them, but I’m glad it explored them. If I had to give one complaint though, it’s that the submarine stages are the only gimmick the game comes up with that don’t emphasize combat in some way, which is odd for Kururin, being a very relaxed series that at the start didn’t even really have a villain to speak of.

Get Kat Koller’s stories in your inbox
--------------------------------------

Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer.

One aspect shared by both the normal stages and the gimmick stages, though, is coins, which also happen to be one of Squash’s newest and perhaps most important additions.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![Image 7: Screenshot from a video game scene with a cartoon character, text, and visual items](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*YXlJpfAMPdJiQrjKPnc21A.png)

Coins can be collected to be used at shops in each world, mostly to buy new skins and HUDs, or for temporary HP boosters or strategy videos for individual stages. While the ability to buy HP boosts is definitely a decent way to give less skilled players some leeway, one could argue that skins being bumped from hidden collectibles to shop items is a bit of a disappointment, and I could definitely understand that.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![Image 8: A screenshot from the video game Katamari Damacy shows gameplay on a level that resembles a river](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*FbN4jLHmIDGsaN9ieIEnGw.png)

But if I’m being honest, I think coins are a very important addition to Squash’s level design. Not only do they allow it to justify having more small hidden pockets to snake around lending stages more play time, but more importantly, it allows the game to more consistently incentivize taking risks, give the player more of a clear path to follow, and generally just feels pretty satisfying on its own.

Speaking of snaking around, I have to give special praise to the controls in Kururin Squash. It’s the first Kururin game to be released on a system with an actual analog stick, and I don’t think it would even be half as good otherwise. For everything Kuru Kuru Kururin and Kururin Paradise do well, I can’t play them without feeling ridiculously clumsy or frustrated, and I think that’s because a D-pad just isn’t a very good fit for the game’s design.

In contrast, the analog movement in Kururin Squash is so precise, there are times where it feels like the level design couldn’t be half as good as it is without the controls to back it up. You still need to hold B to move a bit faster, but in effect that gives you an extra handy way to manage your own speed, which is a good fit for Squash’s level design.

And maybe most importantly, Squash carries over Paradise’s addition of having the right shoulder button speed up your rotation. With the GameCube’s analog triggers, though, this goes from letting you switch between two speeds to making finer adjustments to your turn speed by however much you need at a given moment. Combined with the tighter movement, Squash really does feel the most freeing of the trilogy in terms of how it plays. Just moving around in this game is really a joy.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![Image 9: Alien is angry, wielding a ray gun in front of a psychedelic background](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*6S88hPd0hsIC1Ry63FnQ2w.png)

There is one last addition in Squash, and it’s the boss stages. They’re alright? They generally build around the world gimmicks in ways that are decently fun, but only a couple of them really feel like a strong enough divergence from the regular stages. The final boss in particular is a bit disappointing, but a part of that is admittedly just because the final world’s gimmick is comparatively underwhelming as a whole.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![Image 10: Cartoon-style depiction of bird marionettes in a brightly colored room with different furniture](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*P8aTPvhIpkXkC0vsXY9KuQ.png)

When it comes to presentation, though, Kururin Squash is very charming. It’s clearly not a big budget game, and absolutely not big enough to have much in the way of animated cutscenes, but the way the developers go about this while maintaining the colorful presentation of Kururin is pretty fantastic, opting for a comical paper cut-out puppet theater aesthetic. It’s cute, it works! Holds up better than some other 2004 titles.

The soundtrack of Kururin Squash is also pretty solid, composed by series composer Atsuhiro Motoyama, who may be better known for his work on Umihara Kawase and Battle Bakraid. Most of the music is in a similar low-key, relaxed pop style as the other games, but at the very end it dips into an intense rock style, and the boss theme is a very heavy and bass-y electronic track, both of which call back more to Raizing’s old shooters more than anything, funny enough.

All in all, Kururin Squash is a game I would easily recommend playing. It’s extremely unique gameplay is something I’ve only really seen an attempt to replicate more recently in 2016's Roundabout, and for all of Roundabout’s strengths, I still think Kururin Squash is handily the best game at what it does, just in terms of pure design and mechanics.

Kururin Squash was the last Kururin game to ever be released, but Eighting’s still managed to have a bit of a history since then. Fans of fighting games, Fate, or both might know them as the developers of the 2008 fighting game Fate/unlimited codes, otherwise known as “Fuc”. Their library of fighting games actually extends even further than that, though, as the co-developers of Castlevania Judgment, and developers of Tatsunoko vs Capcom, and Marvel vs Capcom 3. If you’re familiar with trashy licensed anime fighting games, you might even know them for a few, including the classic game that took Super Smash Bros Melee by surprise, Battle Stadium DON.

These days, though, Eighting seems to take more of an assisting role, with their most notable work being assisting Capcom in developing Monster Hunter 3 Ultimate and 4 Ultimate. No need to worry about them, though. They’re just making Kamen Rider games now.

Once again, thanks to everyone pledging and supporting me in making these posts on [Patreon](https://www.patreon.com/colonelreviewsgamesorsomething)! I don’t have any plans to lock any of these posts behind supporting me, so it’s really your own choice whether or not you want to. If you do, I appreciate it, but either way, thank you for reading!

17.title: Kikizo | GameCube Review: Kururin Squash
17.description: Video game reviews, previews, interviews, video downloads and cheats.
17.content:
We get to grips with this fantastic GameCube import release from Nintendo.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------

**By [Jonti Davies](https://www.kikizo.com/#contact)**

Rotating sticks have been amusing mankind since, quite possibly, the Stone Age. And there remains something ineffably amusing about the prospect of navigating mazes. Combine the two concepts and you have _Kuru Kururin Squash_ - a generous helping of concentrated gameplay genius presented in a lovingly sugarcrafted way.

[![Image 1: Video game on a handheld with a small airplane in the center of the screen](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/01b.jpg)](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/01.jpg)

[![Image 2: Kikizo K zoom in-game scenery with a character flying](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/02b.jpg)](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/02.jpg)

Before discussing the gameplay (buck trends), we'd like to give special mention to this little game's little soundtrack because it is quite a treat. The tunes in Squash bear all the hallmarks of classic Koji Kondo cuts, but there's some eccentricity in there which can only have arisen as a result of escalator journeys up and down Kyoto's jingle-soundtracked department stores. These are memorable humalong songs.

[![Image 3: A screen from a video game shows four boxes with Japanese characters above them, with the word READY in the center](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/03b.jpg)](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/03.jpg)

[![Image 4: Video game screen depicting top-down gameplay with multiple shapes and point counters](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/04b.jpg)](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/04.jpg)

[![Image 5: Kirikizo is being played on the Nintendo DS](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/05b.jpg)](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/05.jpg)

[![Image 6: A gameplay screen of Super Monkey Ball Adventure video game is captured, featuring a monkey character navigating a 3D maze with various obstacles and a timer displayed in the upper-left corner](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/06b.jpg)](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/06.jpg)

Now: the game. Those of you who have been paying attention will be well aware of the splendid _Kururin_ Game Boy Advance releases, and if you've had the privilege to play those games there will be little in the series' GameCube debut to rock your world. However, Squash does innovate nicely and is as perfectly playable as its diminutive cousins.

[![Image 7: A colorful cartoon rocket ship surrounded by flying hearts and red-ringed targets flies through a blue and green background in a video game screenshot](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/07b.jpg)](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/07.jpg)

[![Image 8: A top-down view of the video game Billy Hatcher and the Giant Egg, depicting Billy maneuvering through an obstacle course, evading enemies, and collecting points](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/08b.jpg)](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/08.jpg)

[![Image 9: A screenshot from the video game Super Monkey Ball Adventure showing gameplay on a circular stage with a monkey character navigating obstacles](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/09b.jpg)](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/09.jpg)

[![Image 10: Screenshot from the video game Kikiwaka's Run, where a red spaceship is moving down a twisty, colorful lane, attempting to hit various hexagonal objects floating in its path](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/10b.jpg)](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/10.jpg)

Each game starts out with our lovable friend Kuru (a plump tweety bird not dissimilar to one of Kirby's friends) sat in his extremely narrow craft--that is, The Stick--at the beginning of a twisting maze populated variously with baddies, mines, coins, power-ups, switches and springs. The trick--and it's wonderfully intuitive, so don't bother reading the manual--is to make your way around obstacles and foes while being sure to stop off for coins, power-ups and energy replenishment. Which is easy and straightforward in principle, but, in later stages especially, often devilishly difficult in practice.

[![Image 11: Dr. Quack is a robotic duck with orange eyes and a purple hat](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/11b.jpg)](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/11.jpg)

[![Image 12: Video game screen captures, specifically of the “Kirby: Canvas Curse”, which features Kirby, a yellow creature with wide eyes and a purple crown, floating above a wavy sea-like background while surrounded by a line of spiky creatures](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/12b.jpg)](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/12.jpg)

[![Image 13: A screenshot of a video game featuring colorful shapes and numbers on a dark background](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/13b.jpg)](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/13.jpg)

[![Image 14: A blue and orange ball hurtling through a jungle-themed obstacle course in a video game](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/14b.jpg)](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/14.jpg)

The main adventure mode is interspersed with cutscenes which spin a typical children's yarn concerning Kuru and his journey into the unknown. Very nice, and nicely presented too. Time Attack mode puts another spin on matters (sorry) by challenging your rotating stick to speed through tricky courses in the fastest possible time. Both modes complement each other perfectly--yin and yang, salt and pepper, peanut butter and Marmite.

[![Image 15: A scene of a video game featuring water, logs, spiked green objects and purple rocks](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/15b.jpg)](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/15.jpg)

[![Image 16: Screenshot of Kizi's Candymania, a video game](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/16b.jpg)](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/16.jpg)

[![Image 17: A Nintendo DS video game with a blue river running through the center of the screen and the character flying](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/17b.jpg)](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/17.jpg)

[![Image 18: Screen shot of the game Water Rush with four views](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/18b.jpg)](https://games.kikizo.com/media/kururin_squash/18.jpg)

One of the main draws in this GameCube realisation of Kuru Kururin is found in its multiplayer modes. Two, three, or four players can join in races and battles across tight paths, with the screen splitting accordingly. It's not quite in the league of Monkeys and Balls, but Squash does offer some hours of fun for four. And the great thing is, like _Super Monkey Ball_, anyone can pick up a controller and join the fray: this is communist game design, and we bow to Nintendo's regime.

Graphics Sound Gameplay Depth Presentation**OVERALL** 8.0 8.5 9.0 8.0 8.5 8.5
THE VERDICT: _Kururin Squash_ is immediately accessible, then, but it is also addictive and--thanks to a nifty credits-buy-items shop system--it is thoroughly rewarding. These qualities combine all too rarely, so we must heartily recommend Kuru Kururin Squash to all fans of Nintendo's eversweet game style. Lovely.

10.title: S3VydXJpbiBTcXVhc2ggUGxheXRlc3QgLSBJR04=
10.content:
Nintendo's latest has us spinning.
----------------------------------

Do you remember _Kuru Kuru Kururin_? This early Game Boy Advance title was not released in America, so the answer is probably no. It didn't really turn too many heads in Japan either, but [Nintendo](https://games.ign.com/objects/025/025047.html) decided to draft developer Eighteen (yes, the people behind _Bloody Roar_) to make a GameCube version. The resulting title, _[Kururin Squash](https://cube.ign.com/objects/696/696537.html)_, arrived to Japan Thursday. While we're not sure what the "Squash" part of the title refers to exactly, we can't stop playing this thing.Our story begins one day in Kururin Village. Kururin and his family have just returned from a trip around the world. But something is wrong. Kururin notices that while the family left as thirteen, only he and two others managed to make it back. Could it be that the remaining family members are lost and waiting to be rescued? Kururin does what any blue-colored chicken would do in this situation: he boards his specially designed "Helirin" helicopter and heads out to save his family.

For those familiar with _Kuru Kuru Kururin_, Kururin's helicopter is the rotating rod thing you controlled in that game. For those not familiar with _Kuru Kuru Kururin_, here's a refresher. In the GBA original and now in the GameCube version, you move a slowly rotating rod through a maze-like playfield, trying to get to a goal. Hit too many objects on the playfield, including walls and other obstacles, and the rod blows up, placing you back at the level's starting point.

As with the Game Boy Advance title, you've got a few powers at your disposal to help you get to the goal without hitting a wall. Holding down B makes the rod move faster. The R trigger makes the rod spin faster. Springs located throughout the playfield make the rod spin in the opposite direction when struck. Using all this, you've got to navigate tight turns and narrow passages without hitting a wall.

In the move to the GameCube, Kururin has undergone somewhat of a transformation. The game is now in full 3D, with a bright, solid world and bubbly soundtrack giving the feeling that you're in candy land. The 3D visuals affect the gameplay, as the camera zooms out at times to provide a greater view of the action.

Kururin has also gained some new powers. While many of the levels feature Kururin avoiding walls and obstacles in his basic helicopter, a few stages put Kururin in an alternate helicopter for added variety. The first world has stages with Kururin in a helicopter capable of punching; this is good for beating up on enemies. The second world has stages that take place over water, with Kururin making use of a helicopter that can dive below with a press of the A button. The third world sees Kururin's helicopter latch on to a track in a few stages. You're required to aim a flame gun to kill enemies while keeping the helicopter's arms away from collision with walls and obstacles as the helicopter moves automatically along the track.

In addition to guiding Kururin to the stage's goal point, you have a few other goals in the stages. Coins are scattered about stages. By collecting coins and building up your stock of cash, you can purchase extra life, maps for the stages, new helicopter colors and even a mini game playable on the Game Boy Advance. Time is also an important part of the stages. While you're free to take your time through the stages, we're sure many will become obsessed with clearing a stage as fast as possible. Once you've encountered a stage, it becomes available for unlimited re-tries, giving you good opportunity to practice.

Clear all the stages in one of the game worlds and you end up in a boss fight. The three bosses that we've encountered so far have each made use of one of Kururin's special helicopters. Boss fights in _Kururin_ are a bit different in structure from the rest of the game, with Kururin taking on a single enemy and the player having to figure out a weak point on the enemy in order to progress. The first three boss designs will pretty clever, so we can't wait to see what awaits us down the road.

Give credit to Eighteen or Nintendo as you like, but _Kururin Squash_ has proven to be an addictive experience so far -- perhaps more so than its predecessors. Stages are designed to fully make use of Kururin's special means of movement, requiring that you rotate quickly or move quickly in order to clear a curved passage. This isn't much of a surprise, as the Game Boy Advance versions had good level design too. The time component gives the game a racing-game feel, where you memorize each and every corner and plan your twists and turns in advance.

A good deal of praise must be given to the game's well-balanced difficulty. Stages that had us tossing our controllers initially become second nature once we'd cleared the stage or gone on to the next world. The game slowly introduces you to Kururin's new helicopters, giving you a chance to familiarize yourself with the controls before throwing crazy twists and turns at you. Those who don't need such a helping hand can select a hard mode of play, where Kururin's helicopter grows in size, making precise movements all-the-more important.

We're having a blast with _Kururin Squash_, and we haven't even tried the multiplayer modes of play. Up to four players can join in on the fun, racing in split screen or battling on a single screen. If the single player mode is any indication, playing this game in split-screen multiplayer mode will be a riot.

There's no word from Nintendo on a stateside release for _Kururin Squash_, but our four hours with the import have us hooked. Let's hope Nintendo of America will see fit to bring the unique gameplay experience of _Kururin_ across the Pacific.

18.title: Kururin Paradise
18.content:
From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

| Kururin Paradise |
| --- |
| [![Image 1: Game Boy Advance game cartridge of Kururin Paradise has a cartoon drawing of the main character](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/8/80/Kururin_Paradise_box_art.jpg/250px-Kururin_Paradise_box_art.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kururin_Paradise_box_art.jpg) |
| [Developer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_developer "Video game developer") | [Eighting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eighting "Eighting") |
| [Publisher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_publisher "Video game publisher") | [Nintendo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo "Nintendo") |
| [Directors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_creative_director "Video game creative director") | Shinji Hatano Tomonori Fujisawa |
| [Producers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_producer "Video game producer") | Hiroshi Sato Masato Toyoshima |
| [Programmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_programmer "Video game programmer") | Yasunari Watanabe |
| [Composer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_composer "Video game composer") | Atsuhiro Motoyama |
| Series | _Kururin_ |
| [Platform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computing_platform "Computing platform") | [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance") |
| Release | * [JP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan"): December 6, 2002[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-1) |
| [Genres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_genre "Video game genre") | [Puzzle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puzzle_video_game "Puzzle video game"), [action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_game "Action game") |
| Modes | [Single-player](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single-player "Single-player"), [multiplayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplayer "Multiplayer") |

_**Kururin Paradise**_[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-2) is a 2002 [puzzle video game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puzzle_video_game "Puzzle video game") developed by [Eighting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eighting "Eighting") and published by [Nintendo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo "Nintendo") for the [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance"). It is the second entry in the _Kururin_ series and the sequel to _[Kuru Kuru Kururin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuru\_Kuru\_Kururin "Kuru Kuru Kururin")_ (2001). The game was released exclusively in Japan on December 6, 2002. North American and European releases of the game were planned, but later canceled. The game received generally positive reviews, with praise for its introduction of new gameplay mechanics and [minigames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minigame "Minigame"). _Kururin Paradise_ was followed by _[Kururin Squash!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin\_Squash! "Kururin Squash!")_ on the [GameCube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube "GameCube") in 2004, and was later re-released on [Wii U](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_U "Wii U")[Virtual Console](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_Console "Virtual Console") on December 9, 2015, also exclusive to Japan.

[![Image 2: This screenshot shows the Helirin flying through a wavy maze towards a key that unlocks an alternate path. The game's interface displays the player's time, the record time, and Kururin with all three of his hearts remaining.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/9/9c/Kururin_Paradise_Adventure_Level_Screenshot.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kururin_Paradise_Adventure_Level_Screenshot.png)

Kururin piloting the Helirin through a maze to collect a key.

Similar to the first game, the player pilots Kururin in the Helirin, a helicopter that continuously spins as the player attempts to navigate through [mazes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maze "Maze") to reach the goal at the end. If Kururin loses all three hearts in a level, it is restarted from the beginning.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-3) The Adventure mode contains the game's story with 34 levels, some of which are accessed by unlocking alternate paths, and the Challenge mode contains 30 levels with the goal of reaching the goal as fast as possible.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-FamitsuMag-4)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-NintendoDream-5)

[![Image 3: This screenshot features four versions of Kururin with different colors in a side-scrolling stage flying through clouds and avoiding spiked obstacles. The game's interface displays the player's time, with icons of the four Kururins between the start and goal of the stage.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/9/9d/Kururin_Paradise_Multiplayer_Minigame_Screenshot.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kururin_Paradise_Multiplayer_Minigame_Screenshot.png)

Four players in the multiplayer mode playing a minigame involving Kururin flying solo from his helicopter.

_Kururin Paradise_ introduces several new gameplay mechanics, including alternate paths and [minigames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minigame "Minigame"). Keys can be obtained in levels, which unlock secret alternate routes inside a previously completed level. When the alternate path is completed, additional levels are unlocked on the world map.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-HardcoreGaming-6) In the Adventure mode, [boss battles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boss_(video_games) "Boss (video games)") take place at the end of each world, but appear in the form of minigames.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-PlanetGameboy-7) Sixteen minigames are included in the "Mini-Game Paradise" mode, all of which can be played in multiplayer with up to four players using the [Game Boy Advance Game Link Cable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance_Game_Link_Cable "Game Boy Advance Game Link Cable"). A majority of the minigames are based on achieving a high score or surviving a challenge given a certain time limit. One minigame features Kururin outside of the Helirin flying in a side-scrolling stage similar to the Balloon Trip mode in _[Balloon Fight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balloon\_Fight "Balloon Fight")_,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-HardcoreGaming-6) where the player must control the bird to avoid obstacles.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-IGN-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-NWR-9) The dedicated multiplayer modes similarly support up to four players. The racing mode from the original game returns, with players competing against each other to reach the end of a maze in the Challenge mode.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-ClubNintendo-10) Players can give themselves a handicap by increasing the length of their vehicle or remove hearts from their character to accommodate the skills of different players.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-PlanetGameboy-7)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-Manual-11): 23  A selection of [magic tricks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magic_(illusion) "Magic (illusion)") can be learned and performed with the Game Boy Advance system, which are obtained by defeating bosses. Each magic trick has an explanation on how to perform them for others, and after selecting the magic trick, the player must turn their system off and back on to activate it.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-NintendoDream-5)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-Manual-11): 15  One of the magic tricks is a Love Tester, which references the [Nintendo product of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love_Tester "Love Tester").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-HardcoreGaming-6)

Kappado, Tenko, Naporon, and Baron Magic of the Magic Group visit Kururin Village to put on a show. Kururin's family left to see the Magic Group since Kururin overslept and was concerned about his bedhead, but after waking up, he arrives late to an empty venue.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-Manual-11): 3  Assuming the Magic Group kidnapped his family and Teacher Hare with villainous intent, Kururin sets out on an adventure to rescue them.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-12) When first encountering Kappado, he reveals that Kururin's family want to learn magic tricks from the Magic Group, and Kururin has to get them back by beating members of the Magic Group in a minigame.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-13)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-PlanetGameboy-7) After rescuing his father Totorin, it is revealed that Totorin was the leader of the Magic Group, as he wanted to teach Kururin some magic. In the end, everyone surprises Kururin by celebrating his birthday.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-14)

Development and release
-----------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kururin_Paradise&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Development and release")]

_Kururin Paradise_ was revealed to be in development in May 2002 prior to its appearance at [E3 2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E3_2002 "E3 2002").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-15) The previous directors, Hiroshi Sato and Masato Toyoshima, returned as the game's producers. Shinji Hatano, the producer of _Kuru Kuru Kururin_, became one of the directors alongside Tomonori Fujisawa. Additionally, character designer [Yōichi Kotabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Y%C5%8Dichi_Kotabe "Yōichi Kotabe") worked with Yoshitaka Ikeda to create the members of the Magic Group.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-Credits-16) The game was announced in Japanese, North American, and European markets.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-17) An English-translated version of the game was showcased at E3 2002, the first time a game in the _Kururin_ series was announced in the North American market.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-IGN-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-ClubNintendo-10)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-18) This version of the game, however, was not planned for release, and the European version was canceled at a later date.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-ND-19) A Chinese version of the game was developed for the [iQue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IQue "IQue")[Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IQue#iQue_Game_Boy_Advance "IQue"), but was unreleased.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-20) On December 9, 2015, _Kururin Paradise_ was re-released on [Wii U](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_U "Wii U")[Virtual Console](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_Console "Virtual Console"), in which the game remained exclusive to Japan.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-21)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-22) One of the members in the Magic Group, Naporon, makes a cameo appearance in the Eighting-developed _[Master of Illusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master\_of\_Illusion\_(video\_game) "Master of Illusion (video game)")_ on [Nintendo DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS "Nintendo DS").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-23)

The game received generally positive reviews, with the game being considered an overall improvement from its predecessor.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-PlanetGameboy-7) Critics praised the graphics,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-HardcoreGaming-6)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-NWR-9) as well as the abundance of inventive minigames in both single-player and multiplayer modes.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-NWR-9)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-ND-19)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-PlanetGameboy-7)

Many critics claimed the game is much more difficult than _Kuru Kuru Kururin_, sometimes requiring split-second precision to navigate the mazes.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-PlanetGameboy-7)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-ND-19) Regarding the game's difficulty, Kurt Kalata of _[Hardcore Gaming 101](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardcore\_Gaming\_101 "Hardcore Gaming 101")_ wrote "[i]t’s definitely meant for veterans of the first game, but it’s ultimately a much more satisfying experience", relating to the added depth in the level design.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-HardcoreGaming-6) Similarly, _Nintendo Difference_ claimed that while initially difficult, the controls eventually become intuitive and don't harm the gameplay experience.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-ND-19)

Daniel Bloodworth of _Nintendo World Report_ complimented the game's art style, citing it as "cleaner, more colorful and has a specifically hand-drawn look".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-NWR-9) He also highlighted certain minigames such as "Mowrin" for being a particularly clever use of the series' gameplay formula in minigame format. The Mexican _Club Nintendo_ magazine claimed it to be "one of the simplest and most addictive games" they have played.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-ClubNintendo-10) In a retrospective review, Adam Riley of _Cubed3_ described it as one of the best Japanese-exclusive Game Boy Advance games.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-25)

The game sold 3,508 copies after three days.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-26) During its initial launch week, it sold 7,801 copies, marking the only time it would appear among the top thirty Japanese game sales.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-27)_Kururin_ _Paradise_ sold a total of 80,404 copies in Japan from release to December 22, 2003.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-28) It would eventually become the twenty-sixth best-selling Game Boy Advance game in Japan released in 2002, and one of Nintendo's lower-performing titles on the system.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise#cite_note-29)

_**Kuru Kuru Kururin**_ (stylized as _**kurukuru kururin**_) is a puzzle game and launch title for the [Game Boy Advance](https://niwanetwork.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance") in Europe and Japan. The game would later receive a North American release for the first time on the [Wii U](https://niwanetwork.org/wiki/Wii_U "Wii U")'s [Virtual Console](https://niwanetwork.org/wiki/Virtual_Console "Virtual Console") service in 2016, and then on the [Nintendo Switch](https://niwanetwork.org/wiki/Nintendo_Switch "Nintendo Switch") when it was added to Game Boy Advance - Nintendo Classics in 2018. The game would receive two sequels: _[Kururin Paradise](https://niwanetwork.org/wiki/Kururin\_Paradise "Kururin Paradise")_, also for the Game Boy Advance, and _[Kururin Squash!](https://niwanetwork.org/wiki/Kururin\_Squash! "Kururin Squash!")_ for the [Nintendo GameCube](https://niwanetwork.org/wiki/Nintendo_GameCube "Nintendo GameCube").

Blurb
-----

[![Image 2: NintendoWiki logo.png](https://niwanetwork.org/wiki/images/thumb/f/fa/NintendoWiki_logo.png/30px-NintendoWiki_logo.png)](https://niwanetwork.org/wiki/File:NintendoWiki_logo.png)_This section is a **stub**. You can help **NintendoWiki** by [expanding it](https://www.niwanetwork.org/wiki/index.php?title=Kuru\_Kuru\_Kururin&action=edit)._

Story
-----

At the beginning of the game, Kururin's siblings have gone missing. Piloting the Helirin helicopter, Kururin sets out to rescue his missing family.

Gameplay
--------

Players must navigate the constantly rotating Helirin through a series of mazes to the goal at the end. Players have three hit points, and getting hit causes the player to not only lose one heart of health but also add three seconds to the timer. Throughout each stage, however, are areas where the player's health is refilled. Each stage has a record time that can be cleared, and the player can earn a gold star for completing the level without getting hit. Each level also has a bonus spraypaint can or accessory that allows the player to customize the Helirin. The game also features an Easy mode, which makes the Helirin smaller, allowing players to more easily navigate stages.

In multiplayer mode, up to four players can race through levels. The game also features a challenge mode, in which the player can play through additional stages.

16.title: S3VydXJpbiBTcXVhc2ghIEhhbmRzLW9uIFByZXZpZXcgLSBIYW5kcy1vbiBQcmV2aWV3
16.content:
Welcome to Kururin Squash, chock-full of wafers and delight.

Kururin and his famous Heririn are back! ...well, his Japanese-famous Heririn. At any rate, Kururin returns for his third outing, Kururin Squash, which has absolutely nothing to do with squashing things. The basic idea of the game is that you have to guide a constantly rotating helicopter around tricky mazes without hitting any of the walls or obstacles. Previously, the series was only available on the Game Boy Advance.

The first thing that you'll notice about the game when you begin is the wonderful art style. While all of the worlds are beautifully rendered in colourful 3D, the characters are represented by Punch-and-Judy-like puppets on sticks, with additional sticks controlling the arms for expressions. When a character needs to change his facial expression, they'll literally flip around and be completely different. It's a unique, great looking style, and I am really impressed by it.

From what I can gather, the story goes that Kururin and his family win a round-the-world trip. They visit various far-off lands, but when they return home, they notice that everyone except Mama, Papa, and Kururin are gone! Mama asks Kururin to search around the

world in his Heririn to track the missing siblings. Again. Honestly, it’s like the damn kids from Home Alone. Maybe Mama and Papa should invest in some leashes.

The new element that makes Kururin Squash really great is that of new helicopters. There are four of them -- one that allows you punch with boxing gloves at the end of the blades, one that allows you to dive underwater for a brief period, one that allows you to control an on-rails flamethrower, and one that allows you to create tornadoes. These four helicopters have been used to create some incredibly clever puzzles to the regular game. The cleverest, I think, would have to be the dive helicopter. This 'copter adds a new layer of depth -- literally. All of a sudden, you have to think a lot further ahead, because there are sections where you'll have to quickly dive underwater to avoid obstacles on top, navigate through underwater obstacles, and then quickly surface before you run out of air. It becomes even tricker when currents are added to the mix, pushing you along when you want to carefully navigate your way through the levels.

The basic game structure for Kururin Squash is similar to the original Kuru Kuru Kururin -- once you complete a stage, you progress onto the next one. Unfortunately, this means that the secret branching paths of Kururin Paradise are no more, which is a real shame. However, like Paradise, Kururin Squash also features boss battles -- only this time, they really are boss battles as opposed to mini-games. The villain in question is an agitated purple Professor with Doctor Octopus-like mechanical tentacles, so from here on, he's going to be called Otto. Otto pops up at the end of each world, and it appears as though you'll need to use your special 'copters to beat him. The first world has you navigating around a giant cake, trying to punch the strawberries so that they hit Otto, all the while avoiding deadly blocks of chocolate and killer wafers.

The real challenge, though, comes from completing each level perfectly. In previous games, you only had to navigate through a level without hitting its walls to complete a level perfectly. In Kururin Squash, that is simply not enough. Now, you must not only navigate through each level perfectly, but you must also collect every single coin in the level. Coins are strewn about the level and sometimes hidden in secret passages. Breakable objects and enemies also carry coins, truly making this a tough mission. (Thankfully, the analog precision of the Control Stick improves your accuracy immensely when navigating through the mazes.) Boss battles become even tougher, as you must not only beat Otto without getting hurt, but also collect all the coins that shower around the arena once he is defeated. Not to mention that you only have about forty-five seconds to collect them all!

There are three multiplayer modes available in Kururin Squash, but initially only two are available. The third, a GBA to GC connectivity game must be paid for with 30,000 coins (but in all honesty, it's very easy to amass that many coins). The link-up game is an observation-style game which can be played with one to four players. Each player will be shown a Hererin on their screen, and on the TV screen, there are three different, yet similar looking Heririns. Using your POWERS OF OBSERVATION you must select the correct Hererin. If you select the wrong one, you'll be penalized by losing time. At the end, each player is graded according to how far they got.

Battle Mode can be played with two to four players. In this mode, it's a race to collect the most coins in a fairly cramped arena. Coins and powerups drop from the sky, and it's a free-for-all to collect them, as they briefly turn your Heririn into the more powerful punch, flame, or tornado 'copters. I haven't had a chance to play this with four players yet, but I imagine that it will be pretty hectic.

Race Mode also requires two to four players. Race Mode consists of a fairly long track with checkpoints along the way. As you might guess, it's a race to the finish. Players can push each other around, making for some dirty fighting. You only have two hit points in this mode, and when you lose them all, you return to the last checkpoint you passed. Additionally, the Heririn of the lead player increases in size as a handicap, so that other players can catch up.

While the lesser amount of multiplayer when compared to Kururin Paradise is disappointing (but really, could you top mowing a lawn with a HELICOPTER?), Kururin Squash still seems to be great fun so far. The multiplayer that is there looks like it will be fun, and single player is definitely proving to be a challenge, even on Easy mode. While there is little to no English in the game, it hardly proves to be a barrier as navigating through the game is a breeze (you can even enter your name in English if you like). You can purchase [Kururin Squash](http://www.lik-sang.com/info.php?category=79&products_id=5407&) from our partners at Lik-Sang.
